lead: Electronic ignition replaces the contact breaker, the part that burns, wears and drifts out of time, with a sensor and a power transistor or thyristor. The spark becomes stronger at high speed, the timing stays set for the life of the engine, and an ECU can choose the spark angle for every speed and load. Laser ignition goes one step further and removes the spark plug's electrodes altogether, igniting the charge with a focused pulse of light. Almost every car and two-wheeler now uses electronic ignition; laser ignition is still at the research stage.
prereq: You need: Ignition systems: battery and magneto for the coil, the stored energy ½LI² and dwell.

blocks.text: In transistor-assisted contact (TAC) ignition the points stay, but they carry only the small base current of a power transistor, and the transistor switches the coil current. The points no longer arc, so they last much longer, but their rubbing block still wears and the timing still drifts.
A breakerless (transistorised) system removes the points. A trigger in the distributor or at the crank tells an ignition module when to fire:

items: Magnetic pulse generator: a toothed reluctor passes a pickup coil and induces an alternating voltage; the module switches at the zero crossing.
Hall-effect sensor: a vane passes between a magnet and a Hall chip, giving a clean square wave that works even at zero speed, so the engine can be timed statically.
Optical trigger: a slotted disc interrupts a light beam; used on some older systems.
The trigger signal reaches the ignition module.
The module turns the power transistor on, and primary current builds in the coil.
At the firing point the module switches the transistor off; the primary current stops sharply.
The collapsing field induces the high voltage in the secondary, and the plug sparks.

blocks.text: The module also controls dwell. It switches on earlier at high speed so that the current always reaches its limit before the break, and it limits the current at low speed so the coil does not overheat. This constant-energy control removes the high-speed weakness of points ignition.

With an ECU the distributor can go too. In wasted-spark ignition one coil serves a pair of cylinders whose pistons rise together, for example 1 and 4 of a four-cylinder engine; it fires both plugs at once, one at the end of compression and one, wasted, at the end of exhaust. In coil-on-plug ignition each plug has its own coil and driver, and the ECU fires each in turn from its spark map.

Capacitor discharge ignition (CDI) stores energy in a capacitor instead of the coil. A small converter charges the capacitor to a few hundred volts; at the firing point a thyristor (SCR) dumps it into the coil, which acts as a step-up transformer. The secondary voltage rises in a few microseconds, so it fires even a fouled plug, but the spark lasts only about a tenth of a millisecond, against a millisecond or more for an inductive spark, which is poorer for lean or slow-burning mixtures. CDI is common on two-wheelers, outboard motors and small engines.

blocks.where: E is the energy stored in the capacitor (J); C is its capacitance (F); V is the charging voltage (V).

blocks.text: In laser ignition a short pulse from a laser, typically a nanosecond-pulse solid-state laser, passes through a window in the head and is focused by a lens to a tiny spot inside the charge. At the focus the light's intensity is so high that the gas ionises and breaks down into a small, hot plasma, a spark without electrodes. The plasma heats the nearby mixture and starts a flame kernel, which then grows as a normal flame.

items: No electrodes, so no electrode wear and no metal to cool the young flame kernel.
The focus can be placed where combustion is best, for example the centre of the chamber, and one beam can be split for several ignition points.
Breakdown becomes easier as pressure rises, while a spark plug needs more voltage, so laser ignition suits high boost and lean mixtures.
Problems: deposits foul the window, the laser must survive engine heat and vibration, and the hardware is costly and bulky; it is used in research engines and test rigs, not in production cars.

examples.question: A CDI unit charges a 1 μF capacitor to 400 V. Find the stored energy per spark, compare it with the 29 mJ that a points coil delivers at 6000 rpm, and find the average power the charger must supply to a four-cylinder four-stroke engine at 6000 rpm.
steps: 80 ÷ 29 = 2.8, so the CDI stores almost three times the energy of the points coil at that speed.
Sparks per second: each cylinder fires once every two revolutions, so 4 × 6000 ÷ 2 ÷ 60 = 200 sparks/s.
examples.answer: 80 mJ per spark, about 2.8 times the inductive coil at 6000 rpm, and an average charging power of 16 W.

examples.question: A laser gives 30 mJ pulses lasting 6 ns, focused to a spot 50 μm in diameter. Find the peak power and the intensity at the focus in W/cm².
steps: Peak power = energy ÷ time = 0.030 ÷ (6×10⁻⁹) = 5×10⁶ W = 5 MW.
Spot radius = 25 μm = 25×10⁻⁴ cm; area = π × (25×10⁻⁴)² = 1.963×10⁻⁵ cm².
examples.answer: 5 MW peak and about 2.5×10¹¹ W/cm², in the range where air breaks down; the same 30 mJ spread over 1 ms would give only 30 W.

traps: Electronic ignition still uses an ignition coil; what it removes is the contact breaker. Only CDI moves the energy store from the coil to a capacitor.
Wasted spark is not a misfire. The second spark at the end of the exhaust stroke meets no fresh charge and does no harm.
CDI gives a fast, strong but short spark; do not write that it is better in every way. A long inductive spark is better for lean mixtures.
In laser ignition the laser does not heat the whole charge; it breaks down a tiny volume at the focus, and a normal flame does the rest.
Peak laser power is energy ÷ pulse time, not energy × time; with a 6 ns pulse a few millijoules give megawatts.

quiz.q: Name three triggers used in breakerless ignition.
quiz.a: Magnetic pulse generator (reluctor and pickup coil), Hall-effect sensor and optical trigger.

quiz.q: What does CDI store its spark energy in, and what switch releases it?
quiz.a: A capacitor charged to a few hundred volts, released by a thyristor (SCR) into the coil.

quiz.q: How does an electronic module keep the spark strong at high speed?
quiz.a: It controls dwell time instead of a fixed dwell angle: it switches on earlier as speed rises so the coil current reaches its limit before every break, and limits current at low speed.

quiz.q: Why can a laser ignite a lean, highly boosted charge more easily than a spark plug?
quiz.a: Laser breakdown needs less intensity as pressure rises, while a spark plug needs a higher voltage to jump its gap in dense gas; the focus can also sit away from cold walls and electrodes, so the young flame loses less heat.

quiz.q: A CDI capacitor of 0.8 μF is charged to 350 V. Find the energy per spark and the average power for a single-cylinder four-stroke scooter at 7000 rpm.
A four-cylinder wasted-spark system runs at 3000 rpm. How often does each coil fire?
quiz.a: Each coil fires once per revolution (once for each of its two cylinders' compression or exhaust ends), so 3000 times a minute, 50 times a second.

quiz.q: Compare contact-breaker, transistorised and capacitor discharge ignition for a high-revving motorcycle and for a lean-burn car engine.
quiz.a: Contact breaker: spark weakens with speed and points wear, unsuitable for both. Motorcycle: CDI suits it, fast rise and full energy at high speed. Lean-burn car: transistorised inductive or coil-on-plug, because the long spark duration helps a slow lean flame, and the ECU sets dwell and timing.

beyond: Not for the exam. Research engines use multi-pulse and microwave-assisted ignition to light very lean or diluted mixtures, and passively Q-switched microchip lasers small enough to replace a spark plug are being tested. Ion-current sensing through the spark plug lets the ECU detect misfire and knock in each cylinder. Search for coil-on-plug ignition, ion current sensing and laser-induced breakdown ignition.
